The original one-parameter popularity model underpredicted choices of the highest-degree hiddencertainty targets. An exploratory extension adding [log(1 + k)] 2 improved BIC by 269.6 points and retained positive curvature in every hidden-certainty session and leave-one-session-out refit. In visible-certainty sessions, the mixed certainty-popularity model remained preferred over this nonlinear popularity model. The extension therefore describes a stable feature of these data, but was introduced after inspecting the original misfit (Fig. 3B; Supplementary Fig. S2C-E). For hidden-certainty networks, the original one-parameter preferential-attachment prediction is shown alongside the exploratory nonlinear preferential-attachment extension, making the high-degree misfit of the original specification visible. The visible-certainty prediction is from the mixed certainty-popularity model. Observed error bars use a 1,000-draw bootstrap over session-by-headline networks.

The sources ultimately selected reflected these choice patterns. Their certainty exceeded the session mean by 12.77 points under visibility, compared with 0.30 points under hidden certainty (difference 12.47, exact p = .029). Their relative accuracy did not show a clear improvement (2.60 versus 0.33 points above the session mean; difference 2.28, p = .314). Visibility also increased the share of selected sources who were highly certain but directionally wrong, from 16.0% to 22.5% (p = .029). Here, "highly certain but wrong" meant a wrong-side private belief with certainty at least 50. These findings distinguish attraction toward certainty from selection of demonstrably better information (Supplementary Results (Source selection and exposure) and Supplementary Fig. S3).

2.4 Accuracy improved without a detectable benefit of certainty visibility

Across 3,504 participant-headline observations with both reports, mean accuracy increased from 64.42 in Phase 1 to 73.04 at the final Phase 3 judgment. A secondary crossed random-intercept model supported this 8.62-point Phase effect (SE = 0.69, p < .001; Supplementary Results (Treatment outcomes) and Supplementary Table S6). However, visibility did not detectably increase the improvement (Fig. 4A). Observation-weighted gains were 8.12 points in visiblecertainty sessions and 9.11 in hidden-certainty sessions; the session-level visible-minus-hidden contrast used for exact inference was -1.43 points (p = .943). The secondary Phase-by-Visibility interaction led to the same conclusion (p = .476). Descriptive means were weighted by available observations, whereas the primary treatment comparison used session-level summaries.

Truth-stratified tests did not reveal opposing treatment effects hidden by the pooled comparison. Nor were there clear condition differences in certainty change, final boundary concentration, complete final-belief distributions, or change in within-network belief dispersion. These secondary comparisons are reported together in Supplementary Results (Treatment outcomes) and Supplementary Table S5, rather than interpreted as evidence that the conditions were equivalent.

The networks' information costs nevertheless affected reconstructed scores (Fig. 4B). Mean retainedlink costs were 34.47 points under visible certainty and 23.27 under hidden certainty (difference 11.20, exact p = .086). Final gross scores were 59.20 and 65.39, respectively (difference -6.19, p = .229). After subtracting link costs, Phase 3 net scores were 24.73 and 42.12 (difference -17.39, p = .029). The net-score difference combined the higher acquisition costs with the lower observed gross score; the latter contrast was not statistically conclusive. Alternative total-round and final-minus-initial net-score summaries gave the same directional conclusion (Supplementary Results (Treatment outcomes)).

2.5 Improvement was associated with social exposure and selected-source quality

Judgments improved even without social information delivered through the experimental network. Participant-headline observations with no retained outgoing link gained 4.50 accuracy points on average (session-bootstrap interval [2.37, 5.99]). This change could reflect repeated elicitation, private reconsideration, regression to the mean, or information obtained outside the task. Observations with at least one retained source improved by 12.43 points. The linked-minus-zero-link difference was positive in every session (exact sign-flip p = .008) and remained 6.44 points after adjustment for initial accuracy, certainty, headline identity, and order (SE = 1.05, p < .001; Fig. 5B; Supplementary Table S7). Linking was self-selected, so this is an association within the information environments participants constructed, not a randomized linking effect.

Improvement also varied with what those environments contained. Each 10-point increase in the mean private accuracy of selected sources was associated with 2.35 points more improvement (SE = 0.21, p < .001), controlling for selected-source certainty, in-degree, and the participant-level covariates specified in Methods. The association was positive in every session and stable across leave-one-session-out refits (Fig. 5D; Supplementary Methods (Accuracy improvement and sourcequality models) and Supplementary Table S7). Selected-source certainty did not provide a clear additional association after these controls. The quantity of information was not associated with a simple monotonic improvement. Adjusted categorical estimates were highest at three or four retained links and lower at five (Fig. 5C; Supplementary Table S7). These patterns do not establish an optimal number of sources; they underscore why source quality and self-selection must be distinguished from link count alone.

2.6 Own certainty moderated revision toward selected sources

We measured signed disagreement as the mean belief of a participant's selected sources minus the participant's current belief. A step-level regression indicated that the response to this disagreement decreased with own certainty. Holding the other predictors at their reference values in hiddencertainty sessions, a 10-point disagreement predicted a 2.50-point revision toward the source mean at certainty 0 and a 1.52-point revision at certainty 100. The disagreement-by-own-certainty interaction was negative (-0.098 response points per 10 certainty points, p = .002), with the same sign in all eight sessions. Moderation by source certainty and by visibility was less conclusive (Supplementary Results (Belief revision and computational-model diagnostics) and Supplementary Fig. S4).

Revision was largest immediately after social information became available. The first update averaged 13.61 belief points and accounted for 44.0% of total absolute movement; later updates were progressively smaller. This temporal profile provides a further constraint on computational explanations, beyond the association between initial and final beliefs (Supplementary Fig. S4B-D).

2.7 Certainty reinforcement improved compact prediction of belief updating

We compared six models fitted to 9,128 individual participant-headline-update observations with retained social links; final-step metrics used 1,823 observations. The no-update benchmark retained the private belief. Simple DeGroot moved beliefs a fitted fraction toward the source mean. Certainty-weighted DeGroot weighted more certain sources more strongly, and bounded-confidence DeGroot restricted averaging to sources within a fitted belief-distance threshold. Certaintyreinforcing DeGroot first averaged and then increased the resulting belief's distance from 50; the hybrid combined certainty weighting and reinforcement. Models propagated predictions recursively and synchronously through each fixed network, rather than fitting the displayed condition means (Fig. 6A; Supplementary Methods (Belief-revision and computational models)).

Certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized fit and aggregate held-out prediction. Its final RMSE was 27.28, compared with 27.92 for simple DeGroot, and leave-one-session-out RMSE was 27.39 versus 27.99. The hybrid fit was closely similar but required another parameter; its BIC was 5.4 points higher. Bounded-confidence DeGroot reached the maximum threshold, making its full-sample predictions equivalent to simple DeGroot while retaining the additional-parameter penalty (Fig. 6B-C; Supplementary Tables S8-S9).

The predictive gain partly reflected better preservation of final certainty, which ordinary averaging compressed too strongly toward 50. It did not, however, resolve the large first update: the plotted averaging variants predicted initial movements of only about 4.7-4.9 points. Behavioral diagnostics also showed that agreeing sources could elicit no movement or moderation, rather than uniform extremization. Certainty reinforcement is therefore a useful population-level predictive correction, not evidence for a universal individual transformation (Supplementary Results (Belief revision and computational-model diagnostics) and Supplementary Figs. S4-S5). Small points show individual leave-one-session-out (session-fold) and leave-one-headline-out (headline-fold) predictions. Larger symbols summarize aggregate performance with standard errors. C, Full-trajectory BIC difference from the best-fitting model. The broken axis retains resolution among social-updating models while displaying the larger no-update discrepancy. Certainty-reinforcing DeGroot has the lowest BIC; the hybrid is close but more complex. Absolute-movement diagnostics in Supplementary Fig. S4 show the underprediction of the first revision.

Displayed certainty and source selection

3 Discussion

Displaying judgment certainty changed the information environments participants constructed. It increased network density, redirected source selection toward more certain individuals, and increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments. These changes did not produce a detectable average accuracy benefit. Under the task's payoff structure, reconstructed net scores were lower. At the same time, judgments improved more when participants had selected sources to observe, and selected-source accuracy was positively associated with improvement. Together, the findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify information that improves judgment.

This distinction places source selection alongside information integration as a determinant of collective belief formation. Previous experiments show that network plasticity can improve collective accuracy when performance feedback helps participants identify better sources [9]. Our participants instead chose sources without access to their opinions or accuracy, and networks and identifiers were reset between headlines. Popularity provided a dynamic social cue, while visible certainty created an additional basis for selection. The resulting shift toward certainty was much clearer than the shift toward accuracy. This does not mean that certainty was wholly unrelated to correctness; rather, displaying it did not reliably improve the relative accuracy of the sources selected. The experiment therefore identifies the information available for choosing sources as an important condition on the value of network adaptation.

The results extend research on confidence in social learning to the stage at which information becomes available. Confidence can affect advice seeking, trust, and the weighting of opinions after they have been exchanged [15] [16] [17]. Here, another person's displayed certainty affected whether that person's judgment entered the observer's information environment at all. Unlike predetermined endorsement or popularity cues attached to a news item [10, 11, 22], these choices jointly constructed a network through which beliefs could propagate. Because belief direction was hidden during linking, the certainty-directed choices cannot be explained by known agreement with the source.

What participants encountered was associated with what they subsequently learned. Selectedsource accuracy predicted improvement across sessions and alternative definitions of highly connected sources. This complements work on identifying and weighting expertise [25]: in a self-formed network, informative judgments must first be selected before they can influence anyone. It also accords with models in which the value of communication depends on evidence quality and source evaluation [26, 27]. These relationships characterize self-selected exposure rather than a randomized effect of source quality. Similarly, the finding that more certain participants revised less does not establish that more accurate participants revised less, the revision pattern implicated in some accounts of decentralized collective accuracy [3, 8].

The computational analyses describe the subsequent integration stage. Ordinary averaging captured movement toward selected sources but predicted too much compression toward uncertainty. A modest certainty-reinforcement transformation improved penalized and held-out prediction, without requiring strong certainty-based source weighting. The improvement was incremental, and all tested compact averaging models missed the large initial response to newly revealed beliefs. Agreement also did not uniformly produce extremization in the behavioral data. These observations support certainty reinforcement as a compact predictive description while leaving open whether the remaining discrepancy reflects asymmetric responses to agreement and disagreement, private reconsideration, or heterogeneous first-exposure responses. First-exposure dynamics therefore remain unresolved; the model preference does not establish a unique individual updating mechanism.

The score findings add an economic consequence to the selection-accuracy distinction. Visible certainty encouraged greater expenditure on social information without a detectable compensating increase in final gross performance. This treatment comparison should not be read as showing that every selected link was unhelpful: linked observations improved more, but the decision to link was not randomized. Nor does a task-score difference establish a general welfare loss on online platforms, where attention costs, persistent identities, reputations, and quality signals differ. The broader implication is that increased connectivity should be evaluated together with information quality and the cost of acquiring it, rather than taken as an improvement in itself. High-certainty inaccurate sources may be especially consequential where cue validity is weaker or exposure more concentrated, but those possibilities remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated effects here [23, 28].

The design also sets the scope of inference. Randomization across eight sessions supports the reported treatment comparisons but limits their precision; a non-significant accuracy contrast is not evidence of equivalence. Repetition of the same 14 headlines, only three headline sequences, and the resetting of networks constrain generalization to persistent information environments. Certainty was derived from belief extremity, so the experiment concerns this observable cue rather than an independently measured metacognitive judgment. Finally, participants without retained links could reconsider their answers or obtain information outside the experimental network. The positive associations between exposure, source quality, and improvement should be interpreted within these boundaries.

Collective judgment is shaped before beliefs are revised. By changing whom people choose to observe, a direction-free certainty cue can reorganize costly information acquisition without detectably improving average accuracy. The value of self-formed networks therefore depends not only on their connectivity or updating rules, but also on whether the cues governing source selection make informative judgments accessible.

Displayed certainty and source selection

Preprint 4 Materials and Methods

4.1 Participants, stimuli, and ethics

The experiment comprised eight online group sessions, four assigned to visible certainty and four to hidden certainty. Session records identified 286 entrants. Of these, 273 generated behavioral data and 239 completed all five updates for all 14 headlines. The 47 participants who did not meet this strict complete-case definition comprised 13 with no main-task record and 34 with incomplete trials. Primary analyses were not restricted to the 239 complete cases: they used all observations containing the variables required for the respective analysis, including 3,529 private judgments and 3,504 observations with both private and final accuracy. The secondary paired-phase model used 266 participants contributing those 3,504 observations. Session samples contained 22-40 eligible participants after exclusions. Overall noncompletion was 16.4%, without a clear condition difference (17.9% visible versus 14.9% hidden; exact session permutation p = .657).

Participants were recruited through Prolific, were residents of the United States, and had an approval rate above 80%. They provided informed consent and received a base payment of £6 plus performance-dependent compensation. The study was approved by the GATE-Lab Review Board for ethical standards in research (GATE, UMR 5824, CNRS; project 2024-01 and approved extension 2024-01bis). The extension received full approval on March 20, 2024.

All sessions used the same 14 headlines, seven true and seven false, drawn from Butler, Prike, and Ecker [29]. The exact texts, truth labels, and headline-level descriptive statistics are listed in Supplementary Table S1. Headline order was randomized, but only three distinct sequences occurred across the eight sessions; order was therefore included as a covariate rather than treated as eight independent schedules.

4.2 Task procedure and incentives

Each headline began with an empty directed network and newly randomized displayed participant identifiers. In Phase 1 (30 s), participants reported the probability that the headline was true using a 0-100 slider. Judgment certainty was computed as in Eq. 1.

In Phase 2 (60 s), participants viewed the evolving network, could create and delete directed links, and could retain at most five outgoing links. Potential sources' certainty was displayed only in visible-certainty sessions. Sources' belief direction and accuracy were unavailable while links were selected. In Phase 3 (75 s), the final network was fixed and participants completed five 15-s updates, observing at each period their selected sources' previous reports. Participants without retained outgoing links underwent the same repeated elicitation without social information delivered through the network.

No trial-by-trial truth feedback was provided.

Participants were informed that the private report and the final report in the fifth Phase 3 period contributed to performance-based compensation. The four intermediate reports were not directly payoff-relevant. The quadratic score, in normalized units, was where T ∈ {0, 100}.

It ranges from +1 at the correct endpoint to -1 at the opposite endpoint. Each retained outgoing link cost 0.2 normalized units, or 20 display points. With k out i retained sources, Phase 3 net score was S final -0.2k out i . Total-round net score additionally includes S Phase1 ; the incremental social-stage measure instead subtracts it. Retaining five sources therefore yields a maximum Phase 3 net score of zero even with a correct endpoint report. These measures were reconstructed from documented task rules, not reconciled monetary payments. The scoring equation and 20-point link deduction were additionally checked against payoff fields in the original experimental exports; the original frontend source was not available for that check.

4.3 Accuracy, certainty, and belief dispersion

Truth-relative accuracy for participant i, headline n, and update t was

The private report was indexed by t = 0 and the final report by t = 5; improvement was A i,n,5 -A i,n,0 . Accuracy is measured in scale points, not the percentage of correct classifications. Directional accuracy separately indicated whether b > 50 for a true headline or b < 50 for a false headline. Neutral reports were counted as not directionally correct in the primary descriptive measure, with their exclusion used in the above-chance sensitivity check. Group accuracy was mean participant accuracy within a session-by-headline network.

Within-network belief dispersion was measured at each phase by belief SD. The change from private to final SD summarized convergence or divergence independently of truth-relative accuracy; mean absolute deviation and interquartile range were sensitivity measures. Boundary concentration was the proportion of reports at or below 10 or at or above 90, with 20/80 thresholds and exact endpoints as sensitivities. The final incorrect-boundary analysis was exploratory. Complete final distributions were compared by equally session-weighted Wasserstein distances (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Results (Treatment outcomes)).

4.4 Networks and dynamic source choice

The Phase 2 event log stored outgoing-link states. Differencing successive states reconstructed 7,937 edge changes and exactly reproduced the 5,135 final directed edges. Actions were summarized in 10-s bins, together with the share of final retained edges already present. For each of 112 final networks, we calculated connectivity, in-degree concentration, reciprocity, and undirectedprojection measures. Density was the number of edges divided by n(n -1), equivalently mean out-degree divided by n -1. Freeman in-degree centralization was i (k in max -k in i )/(n -1) 2 . The network-example selection rule and supporting topology definitions are given in Supplementary Methods (Network reconstruction and source-choice models). Each of 6,536 edge-creation events generated a conditional choice set comprising the selected target and all other available participants not already linked by the sender. Candidate in-degree was measured immediately before creation. Conditional multinomial-logit models compared random choice, popularity alone through log(1 + k), target certainty per 10 points, and their combination. Models were fitted across all events and by condition and compared using event-level likelihood, AIC, BIC, log loss, and top-one prediction accuracy. Coefficient inference used network-clustered standard errors and two-sided Wald tests; differences between condition-specific slopes were assessed by exact session-label permutation. The exploratory nonlinear-popularity model added [log(1 + k)] 2 after inspection of high-degree misfit. Leave-one-session-out checks and conditionspecific fits assessed its stability (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Results (Source selection and exposure)).

Subtracting a common session or session-by-headline certainty mean from all candidates leaves the conditional-choice certainty coefficient unchanged. Relative certainty was therefore used for retained-source exposure summaries, while event-level models reported the algebraically equivalent within-choice-set slope. These models concern target selection conditional on creating a link, not the decision to create or delete one.

4.5 Source exposure and belief-revision regressions

Each retained edge inherited its source's private certainty, accuracy, and final in-degree. Relative source characteristics were centered on the session mean, with session-by-headline centering as a sensitivity. High-certainty wrong sources had a wrong-side private report and certainty at least 50: b ≥ 75 for false or b ≤ 25 for true headlines.

The adjusted linked-versus-zero-link comparison used ordinary least squares with session-clustered standard errors, controlling for private accuracy and certainty, headline identity, and order. Linkcount analyses treated retained counts 0-5 categorically, with linear models as sensitivities. Among linked observations, source-quality models predicted improvement from mean source accuracy, certainty, and in-degree, controlling for own initial accuracy and certainty, link count, condition, truth, order, and item structure. Source exposure was self-selected throughout (Supplementary Methods (Accuracy improvement and source-quality models)).

For step-level revision, signed neighbor disagreement was where N i is the selected source set.

An ordinary least-squares model with session-clustered standard errors predicted the next signed belief change from disagreement, own and source certainty, source number, condition, update period, and disagreement interactions with own certainty, source certainty, and condition. To interpret susceptibility, we evaluated responses to a 10-point disagreement across own certainty while holding the other continuous covariates at their reference means. A separate final-belief regression and its collinearity diagnostic are retained in Supplementary Methods (Belief-revision and computational models).

4.6 Statistical inference

The treatment-assignment unit was the session. Primary condition comparisons enumerated all 84 = 70 assignments of four visible-certainty labels across eight sessions. Two-sided exact p-values therefore had a minimum of 2/70 = .0286, reported as .029. Truth-specific outcomes were averaged within session with equal headline weighting; condition-by-truth interactions contrasted the true-minus-false difference between conditions. Bootstrap intervals for these comparisons resampled sessions within condition. The certainty-change, final 10-point boundary-concentration, and belief-SD-change family also received Holm adjustment.

False-true baseline comparisons enumerated all 147 = 3,432 headline-label assignments, keeping observations from each headline together. Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance was the primary distributional statistic, with Wasserstein and Cramér-von Mises sensitivities. The additional above-chance checks used crossed random-intercept models and headline-label permutations; the directional sensitivity excluded exact-50 responses to retain a 50% chance benchmark. The secondary Phase-by-Visibility model used centered Phase and Visibility terms, Truth and Order covariates, and participant, headline, and session random intercepts. It did not replace session-level exact treatment inference (Supplementary Methods (Baseline and treatment checks)).

Auxiliary continuous-outcome mixed models were Gaussian. The retained-link-count model included condition, private certainty and accuracy, truth, and centered order, with random intercepts for participant, headline, and session. Its normal-approximation treatment test was secondary to exact permutation. To assess small-cluster stability of key observational associations, linked-versus-zero-link, selected-source-accuracy, and own-certainty moderation models were also fitted separately in each session and in leave-one-session-out refits. Directional consistency used all 28 = 256 sign assignments, with a minimum two-sided value 2/256 = .0078, reported as .008.

Within-network belief-dispersion change was final minus private belief SD, with mean absolute deviation and interquartile range as secondary checks. Boundary concentration was the share of judgments at or below 10 or at or above 90. Complete final distributions were compared using equal-session-weighted Wasserstein distances with exact reassignment of session labels.

The quadratic score can be written as S = 1 -2d 2 , where d = |B -T |/100. If k links were retained, Phase 3 net score was S final -0.2k. We also calculated total-round net score, S Phase1 + S final -0.2k, and final-minus-initial score change net of link costs.

As a secondary descriptive check requested during manuscript revision, a Gaussian crossed random-intercept model used accuracy ∼ Phase * Visibility + Truth + Order + (1|participant) + (1|headline) + (1|session).

Phase and Visibility were centered. The model used 7,008 phase observations from 3,504 participantheadline trials. Its normal-approximation tests do not replace exact session-level inference for the randomized visibility manipulation.

S1.3 Network reconstruction and source-choice models

The Phase 2 event log stored the complete outgoing-link state after each action. Differencing successive states reconstructed 7,937 creations or deletions and reproduced all 5,135 final directed edges. Linking activity and cumulative retention of final edges were summarized in 10-s bins.

The illustrative networks in main-text Fig. 2C were selected by a reproducible contrastive rule rather than visual inspection. Hidden and visible-certainty networks were paired within headline. For each network, a composite score summed standardized total link count, maximum in-degree, and in-degree Gini. The lowest-scoring hidden and highest-scoring visible network were identified within each headline, and the headline with the largest visible-minus-hidden composite difference supplied the displayed pair. The examples illustrate structure and are not condition averages.

For each final network, density was the fraction of possible directed links present. Freeman in-degree centralization was

Additional reported measures included in-degree Gini, largest weakly connected component, maximum in-degree, reciprocity, and modularity.

Each of 6,536 edge-creation events generated a conditional choice set containing the selected target and every currently available unchosen target. Candidate attributes were measured immediately before the action. The initial models were random choice, popularity based on current in-degree k, certainty only, and a mixed model with both certainty and log(1 + k). Coefficient uncertainty used network-clustered standard errors. The exploratory nonlinear-popularity model added [log(1 + k)] 2 after inspection of the high-degree misfit; its stability was checked across hidden-certainty sessions and leave-one-session-out refits.

S1.4 Source exposure and accuracy improvement

Each retained outgoing edge inherited the selected source's private certainty, private accuracy, and final in-degree. Relative source certainty and accuracy were defined by subtracting the corresponding session mean; centering within session-by-headline network was a sensitivity check.

The adjusted linked-versus-zero-link comparison used ordinary least squares with session-clustered standard errors and controlled for private accuracy and certainty, headline identity, and order.

S2 Supplementary results

S2.1 Baseline judgments and headline heterogeneity

Private judgments varied substantially across headlines (Supplementary Table S1). Mean Phase 1 accuracy ranged from 36.1 for news_09 to 85.5 for news_04, and directional accuracy ranged from .309 to .878. Mean Phase 1 accuracy was 68.11 for false news and 60.63 for true news, but this difference was not conclusive when truth labels were permuted across the 14 headlines (p = .341).

The full distributional comparison was likewise not conclusive (KS D = .184, exact p = .105; Wasserstein p = .341; Cramér-von Mises p = .172).

The additional above-chance analyses supported the main-text baseline statement (Supplementary Table S2). Continuous truth-relative accuracy was 64.36; the crossed-model test against 50 gave z = 3.75, p < .001. Directional accuracy was 64.15%, with a crossed-model estimate of 63.97% (z = 2.83, p = .005). Headline-label permutation checks gave the same conclusion (continuous p = .0047; directional p = .0058). Excluding the 259 exact-50 reports increased directional accuracy to 69.24%, with exact p = .0058.

S2.2 Network construction and topology

Action rates fell sharply during Phase 2 (Supplementary Fig. S1). There were 2,669 edge creations or deletions in the first 10 s and 410 in the last 10 s. During the final 10-s bin, 93.6% of participantheadline observations involved no action, and by 50 s approximately 96.6% of final retained edges were already present.

Final network topology is summarized in Supplementary Table S3. Mean density was .057 under visible certainty and .038 under hidden certainty (exact p = .029). The largest weakly connected component contained 87.9% and 79.2% of participants, respectively (p = .057). Freeman indegree centralization did not differ detectably (.154 versus .159, p = .914); the other reported concentration and topology measures likewise showed no clear condition difference.

S2.3 Source selection and exposure

The mixed conditional-choice model showed separable associations of displayed certainty and current popularity with target choice (Supplementary Fig. S2; Supplementary Table S4). A 10-point increase in target certainty multiplied choice odds by 1.016 in hidden-certainty networks and 1.113 in visible-certainty networks. A one-unit increase in log(1 + k) multiplied odds by 1.606 and 1.578, respectively. In visible-certainty sessions the mixed model had the lowest BIC among the initial candidates; in hidden-certainty sessions popularity alone was the best initial candidate.

The initial one-parameter popularity model underpredicted choices of the highest-degree hiddencertainty targets. The exploratory squared-popularity term reduced BIC from 18,654.8 to 18,385.2 and retained positive curvature in all four hidden sessions and all four leave-one-session-out refits.

In visible-certainty sessions the mixed certainty-popularity model remained preferred over the nonlinear popularity model.

The final selected-source composition mirrored these event-level effects (Supplementary Fig. S3). Selected sources were 12.77 certainty points above their session mean under visibility and 0.30 points above it under hidden certainty (difference 12.47, exact p = .029). Relative selected-source accuracy differed by only 2.28 points (p = .314). The share of selected sources that were both highly certain and directionally wrong increased from 16.0% to 22.5% (p = .029).

4.7 Computational models and validation

Models propagated beliefs recursively and synchronously on each final directed network. Parameters were shared across the pooled fitted observations. The fitting unit was the individual participantheadline-update observation with at least one retained outgoing link, not a condition-level mean trajectory. Simple DeGroot mixed the participant's current belief and the ordinary source mean with fitted rate λ; certainty-weighted and bounded-confidence variants altered the averaging weights or accepted source set. Certainty-reinforcing DeGroot applied an odds-power transformation after ordinary averaging, with β = 1 recovering ordinary DeGroot and β > 1 increasing certainty while preserving direction and exact endpoints. The hybrid combined weighting and reinforcement; the no-update benchmark retained the private report. Complete equations and parameter bounds are in Supplementary Methods (Belief-revision and computational models).

Parameters minimized trajectory mean squared error across 9,128 observations; final metrics used 1,823 fifth-period reports. Gaussian predictive log likelihood used model-specific residual SD, counted as an additional AIC/BIC parameter. This was a predictive error model, not an assertion that bounded repeated responses were independent Gaussian draws. Validation refitted models leaving out each session or headline. Marginal-distribution and absolute-movement diagnostics supplemented RMSE and MAE; the model equations and supporting diagnostics are reported in Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Results (Belief revision and computational-model diagnostics).

Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks

It follows the same terminology and samples. "Certainty" is the direction-free quantity c = 2|b -50|, not an independently elicited confidence report. Randomized visible-hidden comparisons treat the eight experimental sessions as assignment units. The study was preregistered before collection of the analyzed data in a time-stamped private OSF document that was not subsequently modified; analyses extending beyond that plan are identified as secondary, diagnostic, sensitivity, or exploratory where relevant.

S1.1 Stimuli and derived measures

The same 14 headlines were presented in every session; seven were true and seven false. The headlines were drawn from Butler, Prike, and Ecker [29]. Exact wording, truth labels, stored high/low believability categories, and headline-level descriptive statistics are reported in Supplementary Table S1.

For a private belief b ∈ [0, 100], judgment certainty was and truth-relative accuracy was where T = 0 for false headlines and T = 100 for true headlines.

Directional correctness required b > 50 for true headlines and b < 50 for false headlines; reports exactly equal to 50 were coded as not directionally correct in the primary descriptive measure. A high-certainty but wrong source was defined as a wrong-side private belief with c ≥ 50, corresponding to b ≥ 75 for false headlines or b ≤ 25 for true headlines.

S1.2 Baseline and treatment checks

False-true baseline comparisons kept each headline intact. The seven false labels were permuted among the 14 headline-level observation sets, yielding all 147 = 3,432 assignments. Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance was the primary distributional statistic, with Wasserstein and Cramér-von Mises distances as sensitivities.

Phase 1 performance was additionally tested with crossed random-intercept models containing participant, headline, and session intercepts. Continuous truth-relative accuracy was tested against 50. Directional accuracy was tested against 50% using the primary coding in which exact-50 reports were not directionally correct. A headline-aware sensitivity check used the 3,432 truth-label assignments; for directional accuracy, exact-50 reports were additionally excluded so that the chance benchmark was exactly 50%.

Condition-level inference preserved the eight-session randomization. Whenever an outcome reduced to one value per session, the exact two-sided test enumerated all 84 = 70 assignments of four visible-certainty labels among eight sessions. Certainty change was final minus private certainty.

Supplementary Information

Link-count analyses treated retained out-degree 0-5 categorically, with linear models used only as sensitivities. Among linked observations, the source-quality model predicted accuracy improvement from mean source accuracy, source certainty, and source in-degree while controlling for the participant's private accuracy and certainty, link count, condition, truth, order, and item structure. Because linking and source choice were self-selected, these analyses are observational.

S1.5 Belief revision and computational models

Signed neighbor disagreement was the current mean belief of a participant's selected sources minus the participant's current belief. A step-level ordinary least-squares model with session-clustered standard errors predicted signed revision from disagreement, own certainty, source certainty, number of sources, condition, update period, and interactions of disagreement with own certainty, source certainty, and condition. The own-certainty interaction was also checked separately in each session and under leave-one-session-out refitting.

Computational models were fitted to participant-headline observations with at least one retained outgoing link. Simulations were recursive and synchronous on the fixed final network. The analysis comprised 9,128 participant-headline-update observations across five updates and 1,823 final-step observations. Models were fitted to individual observations, not to the mean trajectories plotted for visualization.

The no-update benchmark assumed b i,t+1 = b i,t = b i,0 . Simple DeGroot computed with fitted social-update rate λ.

Certainty-weighted DeGroot replaced the ordinary source mean with b(c) where ϵ = 0.001 and γ is a fitted certainty-weighting exponent.

Bounded-confidence DeGroot used fitted threshold δ to define

When S i (t) was non-empty, the participant updated toward the ordinary mean of accepted sources; otherwise the belief remained unchanged.

Certainty-reinforcing DeGroot first applied ordinary DeGroot mixing, p i,t = m i,t /100, then predicted b i,t+1 = 100 p β i,t where β = 1 recovers ordinary DeGroot and β > 1 increases the distance of interior beliefs from 50 while preserving direction and exact endpoints.

The hybrid combined certainty weighting and certainty reinforcement.

Parameters minimized trajectory mean squared prediction error. Predictive Gaussian log likelihood used a model-specific residual SD, counted as an additional AIC/BIC parameter. Validation refitted each model leaving out one session or one headline. Distributional and absolute-movement diagnostics complemented participant-level RMSE and MAE.

S2.4 Treatment outcomes and accuracy improvement

Across 3,504 participant-headline observations with both reports, mean accuracy rose from 64.42 at Phase 1 to 73.04 at the final Phase 3 judgment. The secondary Phase-by-Visibility analysis estimated an 8.62-point Phase effect (p < .001), no clear average visibility effect (p = .527), and no Phase-by-Visibility interaction (p = .476; Supplementary Table S6). The interaction conclusion agrees with the primary session-level visible-minus-hidden improvement contrast of -1.43 points (exact p = .943).

Truth-specific treatment tests, certainty change, boundary concentration, final distributions, and belief-dispersion change likewise showed no clear visibility effects (Supplementary Table S5). Final gross scores were 65.39 under hidden certainty and 59.20 under visible certainty (p = .229), while mean retained-link costs were 23.27 and 34.47 points (p = .086). The resulting Phase 3 net scores were 42.12 and 24.73 (visible-minus-hidden difference -17.39, exact p = .029).

Linked observations improved by 12.43 accuracy points on average, compared with 4.50 points among observations with no retained source. The linked-minus-zero-link difference was positive in all eight sessions (exact sign-flip p = .008); after adjustment for private accuracy, certainty, headline identity, and order, the difference was 6.44 points (SE = 1.05, p < .001; Supplementary Table S7). Adjusted categorical estimates did not show a simple monotonic increase across retained link counts.

In the joint selected-source model, each 10-point increase in mean source accuracy predicted 2.35 points more improvement (SE = 0.21, p < .001). Selected-source certainty did not add a clear independent association (p = .136), while source in-degree remained positively associated with improvement (p = .011). All eight session-specific source-accuracy coefficients were positive (exact sign-flip p = .008).

S2.5 Belief revision and computational-model diagnostics

The response to a fixed disagreement with selected sources decreased with participants' own certainty (Supplementary Fig. S4A). In hidden-certainty networks, a 10-point disagreement predicted a 2.50-point revision at own certainty 0 and a 1.52-point revision at certainty 100. The disagreement-by-own-certainty interaction was -0.098 response points per 10 certainty points (p = .002), was negative in all eight session-specific fits (exact sign-flip p = .008), and remained negative in every leave-one-session-out refit. Moderation by source certainty (p = .097) and visibility (p = .165) was less conclusive.

Belief movement was strongly front-loaded. The first update averaged 12.56 points for false news and 14.60 points for true news, and accounted for 44.0% of total absolute movement. Simple, certainty-weighted, and certainty-reinforcing DeGroot predicted first-step movement of only about 4.7-4.9 points (Supplementary Fig. S4B,C).

Full-sample penalized fit favored certainty-reinforcing DeGroot (Supplementary Table S8). Its BIC was 5.4 points lower than the hybrid, 209.4 lower than certainty-weighted DeGroot, 277.3 lower than simple DeGroot, and 286.4 lower than bounded-confidence DeGroot. Aggregate leave-one-session-out and leave-one-item-out errors likewise favored certainty-reinforcing DeGroot among the compact models, with the hybrid very close (Supplementary Table S9).

The distributional diagnostics address model adequacy rather than ranking (Supplementary Fig. S5). Ordinary DeGroot compressed final beliefs too strongly toward 50. At the final update, observed mean certainty was 79.85 for false news and 75.68 for true news; simple DeGroot predicted 48.29 and 41.73, whereas certainty-reinforcing DeGroot predicted 59.65 and 54.41. Even the preferred compact model therefore left substantial discrepancies. Behavioral checks also showed Supplementary Information that agreement did not uniformly induce extremization: when agreeing sources were less extreme than the participant, mean movement was 1.60 points toward moderation. Certainty reinforcement should therefore be interpreted as a compact population-level predictive correction, not as a universal individual rule.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Experimental design.For each headline, participants first reported the probability that the headline was true (Phase 1, 30 s), then constructed a directed observation network by creating or deleting up to five costly links (Phase 2, 60 s), and finally revised their judgment over five consecutive 15-s update periods (Phase 3, 75 s total). The lower sequence illustrates the evolution of the network during Phase 2. The schematic shows the visible-certainty interface; hidden-certainty sessions were identical except that other participants' certainty labels were not displayed during network formation. Belief direction remained hidden while links were chosen, and selected sources' numerical beliefs became visible only after the network was fixed. The participant-facing label "level of confidence" denotes the computed certainty quantity in Eq. 1, not a separately elicited report. Links cost 20 score points per retained source. The example shown here gives 28 points if the headline is true and 68 points if it is false before link costs, and -12 and 28 points, respectively, after two retained links. Only the Phase 1 and final Phase 3 reports were directly payoff-relevant.

Figure 2.

Figure 2. Network construction, connectivity, and concentration. A, Share of participant-headline observations containing at least one link action in successive 10-s intervals; bands show standard errors across session-by-headline networks. B, Distribution of final retained out-degree by condition, with standard errors across networks. C, Illustrative final networks for the same headline. Nodes represent participants; arrows point from selector to source; node color denotes private certainty and node size denotes final in-degree. This pair was selected by a reproducible contrastive rule, not as representative condition averages (SI Methods). D, Session-level density, largest weak-component share, and Freeman in-degree centralization. Small points represent the eight sessions; diamonds indicate condition means. Connectivity and concentration are distinct network properties.

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Accuracy and reconstructed score consequences of certainty visibility. A, Sessionmean truth-relative accuracy at the private Phase 1 judgment and the final judgment after the fifth Phase 3 update, by condition. The x-axis label "Final" denotes this fifth update. Lines connect condition means; error bars show the observed range across the four sessions per condition. B, Final gross score, retained-link cost, and Phase 3 net score. Boxplots summarize the four session-level values; diamonds indicate condition means. Scores are shown on the 100-point display scale. Net score is final gross score minus 20 points per retained link. These are session-level summaries and therefore need not equal observation-weighted descriptive contrasts reported elsewhere in the text.

Figure 5.

Figure5. Accuracy improvement and the quality of selected sources. A, Private and final truth-relative accuracy, separately for false and true headlines. Boxplots summarize participant-headline distributions; points and lines show means. B, Improvement by condition and retained social exposure. Zero-link observations had no outgoing link at the end of Phase 2; linked observations retained at least one. Violin plots show distributions, with means and 95% confidence intervals. C, Adjusted categorical improvement estimates by retained link count and headline truth, with cluster-robust standard errors. Lines show linear sensitivity summaries, not the primary categorical specification. D, Association of improvement with mean selected-source private accuracy. Points are descriptive means in five quantile-based bins per truth category; lines are adjusted regression predictions with cluster-robust 95% confidence intervals. Mean source accuracy summarizes source-set quality without assuming equal weighting during updating. Source exposure and link count were self-selected throughout.

Figure 6.

Figure 6. Observed belief trajectories and compact model predictions. A, Observed and predicted mean beliefs from the private judgment at step 0 through the five social-update periods, separately for false and true headlines. Step 0 and the subsequent trajectories use the same linked participant-headline sample; all models share the observed initialization. The displayed means are visualization summaries, not the fitting unit. B, Held-out final-step mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE). Small points show individual leave-one-session-out (session-fold) and leave-one-headline-out (headline-fold) predictions. Larger symbols summarize aggregate performance with standard errors. C, Full-trajectory BIC difference from the best-fitting model. The broken axis retains resolution among social-updating models while displaying the larger no-update discrepancy. Certainty-reinforcing DeGroot has the lowest BIC; the hybrid is close but more complex. Absolute-movement diagnostics in Supplementary Fig.S4show the underprediction of the first revision.
